fullBlockReview.assessment: 1911, 荷兰, 卡曼林·盎曼斯, mercury (水银), liquid helium, 4.1 K and figure172 remain source-bound. The discoverer's country, identity and year are corroborated by PRIMARY92-1 and PRIMARY92-3. The precise 4.1 K value is explicitly the source's recorded value, not silently replaced or certified as a universal modern transition constant. Many metals/alloys is not all metals. The added weak-field Meissner description and explicit non-equivalence of ideal perfect conductivity and superconductivity are sound at this introductory level.

20 K and the source's end-of-book appendix reference are preserved. The numerical range is confined to the source discussion and is explicitly not a universal superconductivity ceiling. Material-specific transition conditions are required; neither low temperature alone nor ordinary metallic identity guarantees superconductivity.

The same ring/current/removal-of-power experiment is retained. The ring must remain closed and superconducting, and exact nondecay is expressly ideal and without disturbance or dissipation. The comparison is limited to generally resistive non-superconductors; it does not infer that persistence alone establishes the Meissner property or that every normal conductor has the same decay time.
The original fig-172 identity, empty source figure text and source reference remain exact. No graph pixels, low-temperature trace, vertical scale or drawn transition position are approved.
The caption remains exactly 图 172 with the same ownership. No caption position or appearance is reviewed.

The coil/electromagnet use is preserved. The claim concerns steady current in a maintained superconducting closed coil and the absence of resistive heating, not total machine energy use. Charging magnetic energy and refrigeration are explicitly acknowledged. The ideal/no-dissipation conditions established in block3 remain relevant; this is not a promise of lossless arbitrary time-dependent operation.

The source's categorical strong-field prohibition is no longer taught as a universal limit: loss of superconductivity is conditioned on exceeding the chosen material's critical conditions. A changing magnetic field can induce current; current produces its own field, rather than a static strong field automatically producing transport current by induction. Critical current and field limits are identified as material/temperature/environment dependent, not a single universal current. Strong-field type-II superconducting magnets are compatible with this modern wording.

The memory-device use is preserved as the source's historical technological account and expressly not as a claim about prevalence in today's computers. No unprovided device name, commercial deployment scale or date is added. This review does not certify a particular historical computer implementation absent from the source.

The near-room-temperature hypothetical and system-loss qualification are retained, but the conductor-loss conclusion is still stated for general transmission without a steady-DC/ideal-no-dissipation restriction. Merely maintaining superconductivity and respecting critical temperature/field/current bounds is not sufficient to promise absent electrical dissipation in a cable under alternating or time-varying operation. See SCI92-1.

The source year 1957 is unchanged. The theory is appropriately described as a quantum-mechanical microscopic explanation of conventional superconductivity, not the first-ever theory of every superconducting property or a complete explanation of all later materials. PRIMARY92-3 independently dates the BCS theory to 1957; the modern text does not teach all superconductors as identical to the simple conventional case.

preservationAndPhysicalLogic.temperatures: K is absolute thermodynamic temperature. No Kelvin/Celsius offset error or conversion of the source temperatures has been introduced.
preservationAndPhysicalLogic.perfectConductivityAndMeissner: The current text explicitly distinguishes zero electrical resistance alone from superconductivity and limits magnetic exclusion to suitable weak fields. It does not demand full magnetic exclusion in the type-II mixed state at arbitrary fields. No microscopic penetration-depth or figure claim is inferred.
preservationAndPhysicalLogic.normalAndResidualResistance: Neither the full source nor the full modern n92 asserts that cooling every metal makes its resistance zero, or that residual resistance universally vanishes. No residual-resistance value or guaranteed all-metal transition is supplied or invented. Exact zero resistance is attached to the superconducting case, not to every cold metal.
preservationAndPhysicalLogic.persistentCurrent: Closed topology, maintenance of the state and ideal absence of disturbances/dissipation are explicit. The general resistive comparison is qualitative, not a universal relaxation-time theorem.
preservationAndPhysicalLogic.energyAndMagneticLimits: Steady-current coil Joule loss is distinguished from energy required to establish the field and run cooling. Strong-field capability is not universally prohibited. The general transmission paragraph still lacks the necessary operating-regime qualification identified by SCI92-1.
preservationAndPhysicalLogic.historicalNumbers: The preserved 4.1 K and 20 K source values are not silently corrected. Source attribution appropriately separates a historical numerical account from an unrestricted present-day material law.

findings.title: Qualify the transmission claim as ideal steady DC
findings.currentExcerpt:
原书提出一个设想：假如有能在接近室温、又适合实际输电条件的超导材料，能量沿导线传递时就可以避免电阻造成的损耗。
这仍然要求材料保持超导状态，并满足磁场和电流的限制；
避免导线的电阻损耗，不等于整个输电系统没有任何损耗。
findings.problem: The paragraph transfers the ideal zero-DC-resistance conclusion to general transmission and lists preservation of superconductivity plus magnetic/current limits as its conditions. It does not specify steady DC or exclude dissipative time-dependent operation. Superconducting cables can have AC losses while their material remains superconducting; those losses occur in the conductor itself, so the last sentence about the whole system does not supply the missing qualification. This matters after the correctly steady-current-qualified coil example: the learner can otherwise infer that any superconducting cable below its limits is electrically lossless.

evidence.basis: NIST directly reports superconducting-wire AC-loss reduction as an industry goal in a program covering power cables and grids.

findings.requestedChange: In this modern block only, restrict avoided conductor resistance loss to ideal steady direct-current transmission with the no-dissipation conditions maintained, and make clear that alternating current or varying magnetic fields can still cause conductor losses. Keep the existing whole-system-loss caveat and room-temperature hypothetical. Do not introduce a guaranteed real-world zero-loss claim.
findings.preservationConstraint: Keep the exact faithful source_text, p0223#9 binding, source lesson/exercise files, original identities and all source numerical givens unchanged. No formula, numeric or figure correction is requested.
